Direct Pass@kk Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning

Mahdi Salmani Affiliation: University of Southern California
{salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu    Adel Javanmard Affiliation: University of Southern California
{salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu    Devansh Gupta Affiliation: University of Southern California
{salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu    Meisam Razaviyayn Affiliation: University of Southern California
{salmanis, ajavanma, guptadev, razaviya}@usc.edu
Abstract

Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality and diversity are naturally balanced by the criterion itself rather than through separate ad-hoc design choices. On eight open-weight reasoning models, our method outperforms existing quality-based and diversity-based pruning strategies. The gains are particularly pronounced when the pruning procedure keeps a moderate number of partial solutions for continued generation, highlighting the value of directly balancing quality and diversity during pruning.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex reasoning, showcasing a strong aptitude for solving complex problems that require multi-step logic [45, 21, 52, 18, 15]. To further enhance these capabilities, test-time scaling has emerged as a prominent strategy, where generating multiple candidate solutions for a single problem allows the model to explore diverse reasoning strategies and achieve substantially better final performance [35, 44, 3, 48]. However, a significant challenge in scaling test-time compute is the prohibitive cost of generating many full solutions, which we refer to as rollouts moving forward [33, 23]. Beyond generation, there is also the cost of evaluating the finished rollouts in best-of-NN methods, which score each rollout with a reward model, and this is computationally demanding on a large pool of long reasoning traces [11, 26, 36]. This computational bottleneck, both in generation and in evaluating all NN rollouts in best-of-NN methods, necessitates test-time pruning of partial rollouts before they reach a final answer and terminate. In other words, we generate all NN rollouts only up to a cutoff of TT tokens, keep the kk most promising of them and run those to the full token budget BB, as illustrated in Fig. 1.

One family of methods examines the confidence dynamics of the model during generation, utilizing metrics such as logit entropy or confidence [30, 50, 17, 43]. The underlying intuition is that if a model is overly confident at an intermediate decoding step, extending the reasoning process is a waste of compute; conversely, if the model is entirely lacking in confidence, it is unlikely to reach a correct solution regardless of the additional compute provided, allowing for early termination. Another line of work leverages the model’s internal state, specifically the hidden states of its transformer blocks, to identify which rollouts are worth continuing [54, 1]. By “probing” these internal states, one can predict whether the model will ultimately arrive at a correct solution, effectively framing the pruning problem as a classification task. This allows for the early discarding of partial rollouts that are unlikely to yield a correct final answer. In parallel, a separate line of research prioritizes representation exploration (RepExp) to select a subset of rollouts that cover as many distinct reasoning strategies as possible [39]. By selecting partial rollouts whose corresponding embeddings are dissimilar, RepExp aims to explore a diverse set of reasoning trajectories.

These approaches, however, sit at the two ends of a spectrum, and neither directly optimizes the quantity we actually care about. The problem with probing methods is that the rollouts they rank highest tend to be similar to one another. As a result, the probe may be confidently wrong about all of the kept rollouts at once, and none of them reaches a correct answer. This is the problem of pure exploitation (Fig. 2a). RepExp, on the other hand, finds diverse rollouts, but because it ignores the quality of the rollouts, it can spend much of its budget on rollouts that are unlikely to succeed (Fig. 2b). These limitations motivate selecting the rollouts by the metric we actually want to optimize, choosing the set SS of kk rollouts that maximizes pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k, that is, max|S|=k⁡pass​@​k​(S)\max_{|S|=k}\mathrm{pass}@k(S), which we formalize in Eq. 3. Optimizing this objective directly keeps the selected rollouts diverse enough to avoid shared failures while still favoring high-quality ones (Fig. 2c).

To this end, we propose PKTP (Pass@𝒌\mathbfit{k} Thought Pruning), a pruning framework that chooses the kept rollouts by maximizing pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k directly. The main difficulty is that, even if the rollouts are sampled independently, their outcomes are not independent (conditioned on the partial observation of the rollout). Hence, pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k depends on their joint distribution (i.e., rollouts with similar partial rollouts tend to succeed or fail together). We model this joint distribution with a latent Gaussian model, in which the correctness of each rollout is obtained by thresholding a Gaussian score. Evaluating pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k under this model requires an expectation over the latent variables, so we instead derive a closed-form second-order approximation of it. We show that this approximation is submodular, enabling us to approximately solve it using a greedy procedure to find a subset of size kk. An important aspect of the proposed framework is that the latent model is trained only once and does not depend on kk, and a single greedy pass yields a nested sequence of subsets, so the budget kk can be chosen online at inference time without retraining.

Contributions.

First, we cast pruning as maximizing the pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k of the kept set, and we model how similar rollouts fail together. Second, we derive a closed-form, submodular approximation of pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k that links the probe and RepExp. Third, through experiments on eight reasoning models, we show that PKTP improves over existing pruning methods, especially for moderate values of kk.

2 Problem Formulation and Related Work

Setup.

Given a question 𝒒\mathbfit{q}, we draw NN candidate reasoning rollouts y(i)∼π(⋅∣𝒒)y^{(i)}\sim\pi(\,\cdot\mid\mathbfit{q}\,) from a model π\pi. Each rollout is observed only through its first TT tokens, the prefix y1:T(i)y_{1:T}^{(i)}. We encode this prefix as a representation vector hi=h(y1:T(i))h_{i}=h\!\left(y_{1:T}^{(i)}\right), a hidden-state embedding of the reasoning up to token T. Pruning then keeps k≤Nk\leq N rollouts, runs them to the full token budget BB, and discards the rest. A completed rollout y1:By_{1:B} is either correct or not, recorded by the sign C(y1:B)∈{−1,+1}C(y_{1:B})\in\{-1,+1\},

C(y1:B)={+1,if Verify(y1:B),−1,otherwise.C(y_{1:B})\;=\;\begin{cases}+1,&\text{if }\text{{Verify}}\!\left(y_{1:B}\right),\\[2.0pt] -1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (1)

Here Verify is a task-specific checker that returns true exactly when a completed rollout reaches a correct final answer, for instance by matching a reference solution on a math problem or passing the unit tests on a coding task. We write C⁡(y(i))C(y^{(i)}) for the outcome of the ii-th rollout once it is run to the budget BB.

Representations.

To prune partial rollouts, we need to map each prefix to a vector that captures its essential information. One line of work relies on hand-designed features of the rollout and the model’s internal states, such as token confidence, the geometry of the hidden-state trajectory, or the convergence of intermediate answers. These features are usually very low dimensional [13, 40, 38, 19, 28]. A second line of work instead keeps the hidden states of the transformer and pools them into a single vector [42, 39, 29], and this is the class we use. In particular, we take hih_{i} to be an exponential moving average (EMA) of the hidden states, which has proven an effective pooling operation [29]. Our improvements are thus shown for this class of embeddings, although our framework can be applied to other embeddings as well. Appendix F gives the details of the representation we use.

Objective.

At pruning time the outcomes C⁡(y(i))C(y^{(i)}) are still unknown, since each depends on a (random) continuation we have not yet generated. How, then, should we choose the set S⊆{1,…,N}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\} of |S|=k|S|=k rollouts to keep? Two extreme choices are as follows.

  1. (i)

    (Pure exploitation) Keep in SS the rollouts {i}\{i\} with the highest predicted success ℙ(C(y(i))=+1∣𝒒,𝒚𝟏:𝑻(𝒊))\mathbb{P}\!\bigl(C(y^{(i)})=+1\mid\mathbfit{q},y_{1:T}^{(i)}\bigr), estimated by a linear probe trained on the representations hih_{i} [54], that is, the kk rollouts with the largest scores w⊤​hiw^{\top}h_{i} for a learned weight vector ww. We refer to this pruning policy as Linear Probe.

  2. (ii)

    (Pure exploration) Build a diverse SS, starting from a random rollout and greedily adding to SS the rollout i⋆i^{\star} by solving

    i⋆=arg⁡maxi∉S​hi⊤​(τ​I+∑j∈Shj​hj⊤)−1​hi,i^{\star}=\arg\max_{i\notin S}\;h_{i}^{\top}\Bigl(\tau I+\sum_{j\in S}h_{j}h_{j}^{\top}\Bigr)^{-1}h_{i}, (2)

    that is, we add, the rollout whose representation is least explained by those already chosen, where τ>0\tau>0 is a regularizer. This is the RepExp pruning policy [39].

Neither extreme balances quality against diversity. What we actually want is the set of kk rollouts with the best pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k. Mathematically, we seek the set SS most likely to contain a correct rollout,

Here, 𝟏​{⋅}\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\} is the indicator function, i.e., 𝟏​{T​r​u​e}=1\mathbf{1}\{True\}=1 and 𝟏​{F​a​l​s​e}=0\mathbf{1}\{False\}=0. The objective in Eq. 3 is exactly pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k of the kept pool, the probability that at least one surviving rollout, once run to the budget BB, yields a correct answer. We also assume that the final outcomes are binary, although the same approach generalizes to continuous outcomes, where each completed rollout is scored by a reward model and the goal is to maximize the best of the kept rollouts [10], in which case Eq. 3 becomes a max@kk objective [41].

Related work.

Existing pruning methods score each rollout on its own, using the model’s confidence [30, 13], a reward model [36], or a probe on its hidden states [54, 25], or they select a diverse set, as RepExp does [39]. Pass@kk has also been used as a training objective for reasoning models [41, 8], but not to decide which partial rollouts to keep. Outside of language models, choosing a set so that at least one item succeeds has been studied in information retrieval and Bayesian optimization [6, 34, 46]. Appendix G gives an extended discussion. In what follows, we discuss how such an objective can be solved.

3 Method

There are some challenges in solving Eq. 3: First, we need to obtain the pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k of a given set of rollouts. We address this by learning the joint distribution of the rollouts’ outcomes under a probabilistic model, from which the pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k of any set can be estimated. Second, even with such an estimate, finding the subset of kk rollouts with the highest estimated pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k is a mixed-integer program. We can therefore view our framework as two components, learning the joint distribution of the outcomes (Section 3.1), and solving this mixed-integer program at selection time (Section 3.2).

3.1 Probabilistic model

Let H=[h1,…,hN]∈ℝd×NH=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{N}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N} collect the representations of the NN generated partial rollouts, Qθ:ℝd→ℝQ_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be a learnable mapping predicting the rollout quality, and define Qθ​(H)=[q1,…,qN]⊤Q_{\theta}(H)=[q_{1},\ldots,q_{N}]^{\top} with qi:=Qθ​(hi)q_{i}:=Q_{\theta}(h_{i}). We model the latent scores of the rollouts as

𝐙=Qθ​(H)⏟Rollout Quality+H⊤​𝐟⏟Rollouts Correlation+𝐦⏟Outcome Noise,𝐦∼𝒩⁡(0,IN),𝐟∼𝒩⁡(0,Id),\mathbf{Z}=\underbrace{Q_{\theta}(H)\vphantom{H^{\top}}}_{\text{Rollout Quality}}+\underbrace{H^{\top}\mathbf{f}}_{\text{Rollouts Correlation}}+\underbrace{\mathbf{m}\vphantom{H^{\top}}}_{\text{Outcome Noise}},\qquad\mathbf{m}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{N}),\quad\mathbf{f}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), (4)

where 𝐦\mathbf{m} and 𝐟\mathbf{f} are independent. Intuitively, 𝐙i\mathbf{Z}_{i} is a score of how promising rollout ii is, so the higher its quality qiq_{i}, the higher its score. On top of qiq_{i}, the term hi⊤​𝐟h_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{f} is a random effect shared by rollouts with similar representations, which makes them succeed or fail together. Indeed, for distinct rollouts, Cov⁡(𝐙i,𝐙j∣H)=hi⊤​hj\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{Z}_{i},\mathbf{Z}_{j}\mid H)=h_{i}^{\top}h_{j}, so rollouts with aligned hih_{i} have positively correlated outcomes. Finally, 𝐦i\mathbf{m}_{i} is noise specific to rollout ii.

The correctness C⁡(y(i))C(y^{(i)}) of rollout ii is then modeled by thresholding its score at zero. More specifically, we define the random variable 𝐂i=2×𝟏{𝐙i≥0}−1\mathbf{C}_{i}=2\times\mathbf{1}\{\mathbf{Z}_{i}\geq 0\}-1. In other words, a positive score implies that the rollout is correct, while a negative score implies that it is incorrect. Since the scores are independent conditionally on 𝐟\mathbf{f}, the likelihood of an observed correctness pattern c∈{−1,1}Nc\in\{-1,1\}^{N} is

Pr⁡[𝐂=c∣H]=𝔼𝐟​[∏i=1NΦ⁡(ci​(qi+hi⊤​𝐟))],\Pr\bigl[\mathbf{C}=c\mid H\bigr]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{f}}\Bigl[\prod_{i=1}^{N}\Phi\bigl(c_{i}(q_{i}+h_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{f})\bigr)\Bigr], (5)

where Φ\Phi is the standard Gaussian CDF, and the derivation can be found in Section A.1.

Suppose we have MM training questions, where question mm consists of the representations H(m)H^{(m)} of a pool and its observed outcomes c(m)∈{−1,1}Nc^{(m)}\in\{-1,1\}^{N}. The mapping QθQ_{\theta} is trained by maximizing their likelihood under Eq. 5, that is, by solving

maxθ⁡1M​∑m=1Mlog⁡Prθ⁡[𝐂=c(m)∣H(m)],\max_{\theta}\ \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\log\Pr\nolimits_{\theta}\bigl[\mathbf{C}=c^{(m)}\mid H^{(m)}\bigr], (6)

where Prθ\Pr_{\theta} is the likelihood of Eq. 5 with H=H(m)=[h1(m),…,hN(m)]H=H^{(m)}=[h_{1}^{(m)},\ldots,h_{N}^{(m)}] and qi=Qθ​(hi(m))q_{i}=Q_{\theta}(h_{i}^{(m)}). Solving Eq. 6 directly is hard, since the expectation over 𝐟\mathbf{f} in Eq. 5 has no closed form. We therefore expand each log-factor to second order in hi⊤​𝐟h_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{f}, which turns the expectation into a Gaussian integral that can be evaluated exactly (Theorem 1).

Theorem 1 (Second-order surrogate).

For a pattern c∈{−1,1}Nc\in\{-1,1\}^{N}, let ϕ\phi be the standard Gaussian density, λi​(ci)=ϕ⁡(qi)/Φ⁡(ci​qi)\lambda_{i}(c_{i})=\phi(q_{i})/\Phi(c_{i}q_{i}), κi​(ci)=λi​(ci)​(λi​(ci)+ci​qi)\kappa_{i}(c_{i})=\lambda_{i}(c_{i})\bigl(\lambda_{i}(c_{i})+c_{i}q_{i}\bigr),

Σ⁡(c)=∑i=1Nκi​(ci)​hi​hi⊤,b⁡(c)=∑i=1Nci​λi​(ci)​hi.\Sigma(c)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\kappa_{i}(c_{i})\,h_{i}h_{i}^{\top},\qquad b(c)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_{i}\lambda_{i}(c_{i})\,h_{i}. (7)

Then, as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0,

log⁡Φ⁡(ci​(qi+ε))=log⁡Φ⁡(ci​qi)+ci​λi​(ci)​ε−κi​(ci)2​ε2+O⁡(|ε|3),\log\Phi\bigl(c_{i}(q_{i}+\varepsilon)\bigr)=\log\Phi(c_{i}q_{i})+c_{i}\lambda_{i}(c_{i})\,\varepsilon-\frac{\kappa_{i}(c_{i})}{2}\varepsilon^{2}+O(|\varepsilon|^{3}), (8)

and replacing each log-factor of Pr⁡[𝐂=c∣H]\Pr[\mathbf{C}=c\mid H] in Eq. 5 by this expansion at ε=hi⊤​𝐟\varepsilon=h_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{f} gives

Pr~[𝐂=c∣H]=(∏i=1NΦ(ciqi))det(Id+Σ(c))−1/2exp(12b(c)⊤(Id+Σ(c))−1b(c)).\widetilde{\Pr}[\mathbf{C}=c\mid H]=\Bigl(\prod_{i=1}^{N}\Phi(c_{i}q_{i})\Bigr)\det\bigl(I_{d}+\Sigma(c)\bigr)^{-1/2}\exp\Bigl(\frac{1}{2}\,b(c)^{\top}\bigl(I_{d}+\Sigma(c)\bigr)^{-1}b(c)\Bigr). (9)

The proof is in Section B.1.1. The expansion is local, so we use Eq. 9 as a tractable surrogate rather than as an exact identity or a bound. We therefore replace Prθ\Pr_{\theta} in Eq. 6 by Pr~θ\widetilde{\Pr}_{\theta}.

Instead of using hih_{i} directly in the correlation term, one could learn an encoder ℰψ\mathcal{E}_{\psi} of the representations and use ℰψ​(hi)\mathcal{E}_{\psi}(h_{i}) in its place, but its helpfulness depends on the amount of data. Since our data is limited, we keep hih_{i} fixed, so that QθQ_{\theta} is the only learned component, and for the same reason we use a simple linear model Qθ​(h)=θ⊤​h+θ0Q_{\theta}(h)=\theta^{\top}h+\theta_{0} for QθQ_{\theta}, as in the Linear Probe [54]. Unlike the Linear Probe, which is trained on the correctness of each rollout separately, QθQ_{\theta} is trained on the joint outcomes of all rollouts of a question, so the quality it learns already accounts for the correlation between them. Since Eq. 9 is in closed form and differentiable in θ\theta, we maximize the surrogate likelihood by stochastic gradient ascent over the training questions.

3.2 Subset selection

Maximizing pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k in Eq. 3 is the same as minimizing the probability that every kept rollout fails. Under the latent Gaussian model, and suppressing the conditioning on HH, the failure probability of a set SS of kept rollouts is

L(S)=Pr[𝐂i=−1∀i∈S]=𝔼𝐟∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)[∏i∈SΦ(−(qi+hi⊤𝐟))],L(S)=\Pr\bigl[\mathbf{C}_{i}=-1\ \forall i\in S\bigr]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{f}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})}\Bigl[\prod_{i\in S}\Phi\bigl(-(q_{i}+h_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{f})\bigr)\Bigr], (10)

and we seek the set of kk rollouts that minimizes it. Since L⁡(S)L(S) has no closed form, we approximate it with Theorem 1.

Corollary 1 (Selection surrogate).

For a set S⊆[N]:={1,…,N}S\subseteq[N]:=\{1,\ldots,N\}, let λi=ϕ⁡(qi)/Φ⁡(−qi)\lambda_{i}=\phi(q_{i})/\Phi(-q_{i}), κi=λi​(λi−qi)\kappa_{i}=\lambda_{i}(\lambda_{i}-q_{i}), ΣS=∑i∈Sκi​hi​hi⊤\Sigma_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}\kappa_{i}\,h_{i}h_{i}^{\top} and bS=∑i∈Sλi​hib_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}\,h_{i}. Applying Theorem 1 to the rollouts in SS with ci=−1c_{i}=-1 for every i∈Si\in S gives a surrogate L~​(S)\widetilde{L}(S) of L⁡(S)L(S) with

log⁡L~​(S)=∑i∈Slog⁡Φ⁡(−qi)⏟Rollout Quality+(−12logdet(Id+ΣS)+12bS⊤(Id+ΣS)−1bS)⏟Rollouts Correlation.\log\widetilde{L}(S)=\underbrace{\sum_{i\in S}\log\Phi(-q_{i})}_{\textnormal{Rollout Quality}}\;+\;\underbrace{\vphantom{\sum_{i\in S}}\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2}\log\det(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})+\frac{1}{2}\,b_{S}^{\top}(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})^{-1}b_{S}\Bigr)}_{\textnormal{Rollouts Correlation}}. (11)

The proof is in Section B.1.2. We therefore minimize log⁡L~​(S)\log\widetilde{L}(S) over |S|=k|S|=k. Each term of Eq. 11 has a direct interpretation. The first term favors large qiq_{i}, because the baseline failure factor Φ⁡(−qi)\Phi(-q_{i}) decreases with qiq_{i}. The negative log-determinant rewards a collection of hih_{i}’s that covers several directions instead of repeatedly selecting the same direction. The last term is nonnegative and penalizes sets whose weighted vectors λi​hi\lambda_{i}h_{i} add up in the same direction, which the determinant alone cannot detect since it treats hih_{i} and −hi-h_{i} identically. For example, two rollouts of the same quality fail together more often with h2=h1h_{2}=h_{1} than with h2=−h1h_{2}=-h_{1}, yet both cases give the same ΣS\Sigma_{S} and hence the same determinant, while bSb_{S} is 2​λ1​h12\lambda_{1}h_{1} in the first case and 00 in the second.

However, minimizing log⁡L~​(S)\log\widetilde{L}(S) exactly is hard.

Proposition 1 (Hardness of exact selection).

Minimizing log⁡L~​(S)\log\widetilde{L}(S) over all S⊆[N]S\subseteq[N] with |S|=k|S|=k is NP-hard.

The proof is in Section B.3, by a reduction from the maximum independent set problem. When the objective is monotone and submodular, however, a greedy optimizer that adds one rollout at a time is guaranteed to achieve at least a (1−e−1)(1-e^{-1}) fraction of the optimal value [32]. The exact pass probability P⁡(S):=1−L⁡(S)P(S):=1-L(S) is known to be monotone and submodular [46]. An approximation of a submodular function, though, is not necessarily submodular, so we prove that its surrogate P~​(S):=1−L~​(S)\widetilde{P}(S):=1-\widetilde{L}(S) is also monotone and submodular, and hence the greedy optimizer and its approximation guarantee apply to our problem.

Theorem 2 (Greedy guarantee).

P~\widetilde{P} is normalized (P~​(∅)=0\widetilde{P}(\varnothing)=0), monotone (P~​(A)≤P~​(B)\widetilde{P}(A)\leq\widetilde{P}(B) whenever A⊆BA\subseteq B), and submodular, that is, for all A⊆B⊆[N]A\subseteq B\subseteq[N] and j∉Bj\notin B,

P~​(A∪{j})−P~​(A)≥P~​(B∪{j})−P~​(B).\widetilde{P}(A\cup\{j\})-\widetilde{P}(A)\geq\widetilde{P}(B\cup\{j\})-\widetilde{P}(B). (12)

Consequently, the set SkgreedyS_{k}^{\mathrm{greedy}} obtained by adding, kk times, the candidate that most increases P~\widetilde{P} satisfies

P~​(Skgreedy)≥(1−e−1)​max|S|≤k​P~​(S).\widetilde{P}(S_{k}^{\mathrm{greedy}})\geq(1-e^{-1})\max_{|S|\leq k}\widetilde{P}(S). (13)

The proof is in Section B.2.

Greedy optimization.

The greedy optimizer starts from the empty set and, at each step, adds the candidate j∉Sj\notin S with the smallest change Δj​(S)=log⁡L~​(S∪{j})−log⁡L~​(S)\Delta_{j}(S)=\log\widetilde{L}(S\cup\{j\})-\log\widetilde{L}(S). Since adding a candidate changes ΣS\Sigma_{S} by a rank-one matrix, this change has a closed form that can be updated cheaply without rebuilding the determinant and the inverse (Section A.2). With these rank-one updates, the greedy optimizer costs O⁡(k⁡(N​d+d2))O\bigl(k(Nd+d^{2})\bigr) time and O⁡(N​d+d2)O(Nd+d^{2}) memory. By comparison, a naive implementation that rebuilds and factorizes Id+ΣS∪{j}I_{d}+\Sigma_{S\cup\{j\}} for every candidate costs O⁡(d3)O(d^{3}) per candidate, that is, O⁡(k​N​d3)O(kNd^{3}) time, with the same O⁡(N​d+d2)O(Nd+d^{2}) memory.

3.3 Relation to Linear Probe and RepExp

The surrogate makes the quality–diversity trade-off explicit and connects to the two baseline criteria in limiting regimes. If the correlation term in Eq. 11 is switched off, then log⁡L~​(S)=∑i∈Slog⁡Φ⁡(−qi)\log\widetilde{L}(S)=\sum_{i\in S}\log\Phi(-q_{i}), so minimizing it keeps the kk largest quality scores and recovers a quality-only, probe-style ranking; it coincides with Linear Probe when QθQ_{\theta} is the corresponding linear probe. At the other extreme, suppose that the quality scores are equal and that the penalty term is negligible throughout selection. Then every κi\kappa_{i} equals a common value κ\kappa, so ΣS=κ​∑i∈Shi​hi⊤\Sigma_{S}=\kappa\sum_{i\in S}h_{i}h_{i}^{\top} and the relevant set-dependent term is −12logdet(Id+ΣS)-\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S}). By the matrix determinant lemma, its greedy marginal ranks a candidate jj by hj⊤​(Id+ΣS)−1​hjh_{j}^{\top}(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})^{-1}h_{j}, the residual-variance criterion used by RepExp on the same representations (see Section A.3 for the derivation). Between these limits, the modular quality, log-determinant diversity, and penalty terms jointly determine the selected set.

The above two extremes do not show how PKTP moves from Linear Probe to RepExp as kk grows. To see this, we expand log⁡L⁡(S)\log L(S) and its surrogate when the correlations are weak.

Proposition 2 (Weak correlations).

Fix SS, qiq_{i} and hih_{i}, and replace 𝐟\mathbf{f} by ρ​𝐟\rho\,\mathbf{f}. As ρ→0\rho\to 0,

log⁡L⁡(S)=∑i∈S[log⁡Φ⁡(−qi)+ρ22​λi​qi​‖hi‖2]+ρ2​∑i<j∈Sλi​λj​hi⊤​hj+O⁡(ρ4),\log L(S)=\sum_{i\in S}\Bigl[\log\Phi(-q_{i})+\tfrac{\rho^{2}}{2}\lambda_{i}q_{i}\|h_{i}\|^{2}\Bigr]+\rho^{2}\sum_{i<j\in S}\lambda_{i}\lambda_{j}\,h_{i}^{\top}h_{j}+O(\rho^{4}), (14)

and log⁡L~​(S)\log\widetilde{L}(S) has the same expansion.

Proposition 2 shows how the correlation strength ρ\rho controls where PKTP sits between the two baselines. At ρ=0\rho=0 the rollouts are independent, the expansion reduces to ∑i∈Slog⁡Φ⁡(−qi)\sum_{i\in S}\log\Phi(-q_{i}), and PKTP ranks the rollouts by quality, as Linear Probe does. For ρ>0\rho>0, every pair of kept rollouts adds a penalty ρ2​λi​λj​hi⊤​hj\rho^{2}\lambda_{i}\lambda_{j}h_{i}^{\top}h_{j}, which is large when their representations are similar. A rollout added to a set of tt rollouts pays tt such penalties, so the first pick is decided by quality alone, and as the set grows the penalties add up until they outweigh the differences in quality, after which PKTP spreads its picks out, as RepExp does. The larger ρ\rho is, the sooner this happens, so ρ\rho sets how fast PKTP moves from Linear Probe to RepExp as kk grows.

Appendix C makes the two ends of this behavior precise for a fixed ρ\rho. At small kk, if the gap between the kkth and (k+1)(k+1)th largest qualities exceeds a constant multiple of k​ρ2k\rho^{2}, PKTP keeps exactly the kk candidates with the largest qiq_{i}, as Linear Probe does, and in the same order when this holds at every budget up to kk. At large kk, when a few candidates of high quality stand out from a bulk of lower quality, the objective of PKTP, averaged over the bulk qualities, reduces to the RepExp objective plus a term for these candidates. Its minimizers therefore keep them and nearly maximize the RepExp objective. Finally, the conditions of these two results do not conflict. We construct a single model, with one quality distribution and one value of ρ\rho, in which PKTP follows Linear Probe at small kk, while its averaged objective reduces to the RepExp objective as kk grows.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

Models.

We evaluate on eight open-weight reasoning models in two size tiers. The small tier is Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B [49], OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B [31] and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B [15], and the large tier is Qwen3-8B, OpenMath-Nemotron-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Skywork-OR1-Math-7B [16]. Every model generates its rollouts with temperature 0.80.8, top-pp of 0.950.95, and a full token budget of B=32,768B=32{,}768 tokens.

Datasets.

We pool problems from several benchmark sources rather than a single one, since a pruning policy has to be trained on part of the problems and evaluated on the rest, and no single competition benchmark is large enough for both. The two model tiers are evaluated on different benchmark substrates, chosen so that neither tier is saturated. Both tiers use AIME 2024, 2025 and 2026 and HMMT 2024, 2025 and 2026 [2], together with RIMO-N [9]. The small tier adds BeyondAIME [4], OlymMATH (Easy) [37] and Omni-MATH levels 7 and 8 [14], while the large tier replaces these by AMO-Bench [27], OlymMATH (Hard) and Omni-MATH levels 8 and 9. This gives around 600600 problems per model. For each model we then remove the problems on which it generates all correct or all wrong solutions in 128128 trials.

Verification.

A completed rollout counts as correct when its final answer matches the reference answer of the problem. We take that answer from the \boxed{} expression of the rollout and ask a Qwen3-32B judge [49] whether it is equivalent to the reference answer. We use a judge rather than a symbolic checker such as math-verify [24], because benchmarks like AMO-Bench have descriptive answers that a symbolic checker cannot handle.

Evaluation.

Only a few hundred problems are available for each model, so a single split into training and test problems would leave too few on either side, and we evaluate with cross-validation instead. For each model we partition its problems into eight folds, with each benchmark spread evenly across the folds. Each fold serves once as the test set while the learned components are trained on the other seven, so every problem is scored exactly once by a model that was not trained on it. One such pass over all eight folds forms a repetition. Because the outcome of a repetition depends on how the problems happen to be divided, we run 2020 repetitions, each with a new random partition obtained by shuffling the problems of every benchmark before assigning them to folds, and with fresh random seeds for training. Every reported number is the average over the 2020 repetitions, and its standard error is computed across them. For RepExp we set the regularizer to τ=1\tau=1. For all methods, the representation hih_{i} of a partial rollout is the EMA of its hidden states with rate 10−310^{-3}.

4.2 Experimental Evaluation and Comparison

Figure 3 reports our main setting, in which each method selects k∈{1,2,4,8,16}k\in\{1,2,4,8,16\} of the N=128N=128 rollouts of a problem from their prefixes, and we set the cutoff threshold to T=4000T=4000 tokens. For every model it shows the pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k of each pruning policy minus that of Random (Pass@kk), pooled over all test problems. Random keeps kk rollouts chosen uniformly at random, which is equivalent to sampling kk rollouts without any pruning, so it is the natural reference point. The absolute numbers are given in Table 1 and the breakdown by benchmark in Appendix D.

As evident in Fig. 3, the Linear Probe performs strongly at k=1k=1, but as kk increases it gets closer and closer to Random, as in the Qwen models, and in some cases it even becomes worse than Random at large kk. This can be attributed to a bias towards a cluster of rollouts that the model predicts to be correct but that may not be, in the case where the classifier is wrong. In other words, ranking by the probe sharpens the distribution of the kept rollouts around what the probe considers correct. This mirrors the effect observed in reinforcement learning, where models trained with GRPO outperform their base models at small kk but are outperformed by them at large kk [53]. As an example, Fig. 4 shows the 128128 rollouts of one problem (Qwen3-8B, AMO-Bench), projected on the first two principal components of their representations. The 1616 rollouts ranked highest by the probe are all close to each other and all wrong, while 1616 random picks include 77 correct ones.

Figure 3 also shows that RepExp behaves in the opposite way to the Linear Probe. At k=1k=1 it shows, as expected, a performance similar to Random, since its first pick is random. As kk increases, the general trend is that RepExp gets better and better than Random, especially at k=16k=16 (e.g., the DeepSeek-R1-Distill models). Interestingly, however, for moderate kk it is sometimes outperformed by Random, for instance on OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B and Qwen3-8B. We attribute this to a tendency of RepExp to favor outliers at small and moderate kk, since the rollouts farthest from those already selected are often unusual rollouts that are unlikely to be correct. A similar effect is reported by Tuyls et al. [39], where RepExp stops helping under high-temperature sampling, since the less coherent responses look novel in representation space yet do not necessarily contain correct answers. As an example, Fig. 5 shows the 128128 rollouts of one problem (Qwen3-8B, Omni-MATH), embedded in two dimensions with multidimensional scaling on their representations. After its first, random pick, RepExp selects outliers far from the other rollouts, and all 44 of its picks are wrong, while 44 random picks include 11 correct one.

Finally, Fig. 3 shows that PKTP outperforms both the Linear Probe and RepExp, and its advantage is clearest at moderate kk, where each baseline suffers from its own bias. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at k=4k=4, for example, PKTP is 3.03.0 points above the Linear Probe and 3.23.2 points above RepExp. On Qwen3-0.6B it leads both baselines by more than 22 points at every k≥2k\geq 2, and on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B it is 3.33.3 points above the Linear Probe at k=4k=4. Unlike the two baselines, PKTP also stays above Random on every model for k≥2k\geq 2, since it keeps the correctness signal of the probe while spreading the kept rollouts over outcomes that are unlikely to fail together. At large kk, however, the performance of PKTP and RepExp gets closer. We believe this is due to the weak correctness signal in the embeddings of the partial rollouts, which raises the question of how a quality embedding can be obtained from a partial rollout, and whether this is possible at all.

Results for the other pool sizes, N∈{32,48,64,80,96,112}N\in\{32,48,64,80,96,112\} with the same cutoff T=4000T=4000, are given in Appendix E.

4.3 Effect of the cutoff threshold

An important aspect of pruning is the cutoff threshold TT, and how the algorithm behaves as the cutoff grows. Figure 6 varies TT on Qwen3-1.7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. For every T≥4000T\geq 4000, PKTP outperforms all other methods on both models. An interesting observation is that a later cutoff in general improves the performance of PKTP. On Qwen3-1.7B its pass@44 rises from 63.5%63.5\% at T=2000T=2000 to 65.9%65.9\% at T=8000T=8000, and on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B from 57.4%57.4\% to 61.7%61.7\%. Intuitively, the more tokens are generated, the more is revealed about the quality of a rollout and where it is heading, so there is more signal to exploit. Interestingly, however, the same does not necessarily happen for the Linear Probe and RepExp. On Qwen3-1.7B, for example, the Linear Probe drifts down from 64.2%64.2\% to 62.3%62.3\% and ends below Random. One reason can be the representation we use. Since the EMA with rate 10−310^{-3} effectively averages over the last 10001000 tokens, it may lose the signal in the earlier tokens.

4.4 Effect of the pool size

Another important aspect of pruning is the size NN of the pool the kk rollouts are chosen from. Figure 7 varies NN on Qwen3-1.7B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. PKTP outperforms all other methods for every NN on Qwen3-1.7B, and on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B once the pool reaches N=80N=80. A larger pool offers more candidates to choose from, and on Qwen3-1.7B both baselines benefit from it, with RepExp rising from 62.9%62.9\% at N=32N=32 to 63.9%63.9\% at N=128N=128 as the pool becomes more diverse and the Linear Probe from 62.1%62.1\% to 63.1%63.1\%. Interestingly, however, the same does not hold on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, where the Linear Probe falls from 58.1%58.1\% to 56.4%56.4\% and stays below Random for every NN, and RepExp falls from 59.5%59.5\% at N=48N=48 to 58.6%58.6\%, while PKTP rises from 58.8%58.8\% to 59.7%59.7\%. One reason can be that a larger pool also contains more outliers, which raises the chance that extreme cases like RepExp and the Linear Probe select them at a moderate kk such as k=4k=4.

5 Conclusion

We introduced PKTP, a pruning framework that chooses which partial rollouts to keep by directly optimizing pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k. PKTP learns the joint distribution of the rollouts’ outcomes with a latent Gaussian model, approximates the resulting likelihood in closed form, and selects the kept set greedily, with an approximation guarantee on the surrogate objective. Across eight reasoning models, it outperforms both quality-based and diversity-based pruning, and the gains are largest at moderate kk, where each of these baselines suffers from its own bias. Since PKTP can be combined with any representation of partial rollouts, representations that better capture the correctness of a rollout would directly strengthen it, and developing them is a natural direction for future work.

Appendix A Derivations

A.1 The likelihood

Write 𝐙i=qi+𝐦i+hi⊤​𝐟\mathbf{Z}_{i}=q_{i}+\mathbf{m}_{i}+h_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{f}. Conditioned on 𝐟\mathbf{f}, the 𝐙i\mathbf{Z}_{i} are independent of each other, so

Pr[𝐂1=c1,…,𝐂N=cN∣𝐟]\displaystyle\Pr\left[\mathbf{C}_{1}=c_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{C}_{N}=c_{N}\mid\mathbf{f}\right] =∏i=1NPr⁡[ci​𝐙i≥0∣𝐟]\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\Pr[c_{i}\mathbf{Z}_{i}\geq 0\mid\mathbf{f}] (15)
=∏i=1NPr⁡[ci​(qi+𝐦i+hi⊤​𝐟)≥0∣𝐟]\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\Pr[c_{i}(q_{i}+\mathbf{m}_{i}+h_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{f})\geq 0\mid\mathbf{f}] (16)
=∏i=1NPr⁡[ci​𝐦i≥−ci​(qi+hi⊤​𝐟)∣𝐟].\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\Pr[c_{i}\mathbf{m}_{i}\geq-c_{i}(q_{i}+h_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{f})\mid\mathbf{f}]. (17)

Since the standard Gaussian is symmetric about 00, −ci​𝐦i-c_{i}\mathbf{m}_{i} follows the same distribution as 𝐦i\mathbf{m}_{i}, and with Φ(x):=PrZ∼𝒩⁡(0,1)[Z≤x]\Phi(x):=\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[Z\leq x] each factor equals Φ⁡(ci​(qi+hi⊤​𝐟))\Phi\bigl(c_{i}(q_{i}+h_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{f})\bigr). Taking the expectation with respect to 𝐟\mathbf{f} on both sides gives Eq. 5.

A.2 Rank-one greedy updates

As in Corollary 1, let ΣS=∑i∈Sκi​hi​hi⊤\Sigma_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}\kappa_{i}h_{i}h_{i}^{\top} and bS=∑i∈Sλi​hib_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}h_{i}. Write ΩS=(Id+ΣS)−1\Omega_{S}=(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})^{-1}, rj=hj⊤​ΩS​hjr_{j}=h_{j}^{\top}\Omega_{S}h_{j} and uj=hj⊤​ΩS​bSu_{j}=h_{j}^{\top}\Omega_{S}b_{S}. Adding a candidate j∉Sj\notin S changes ΣS\Sigma_{S} by the rank-one matrix κj​hj​hj⊤\kappa_{j}h_{j}h_{j}^{\top}. The matrix determinant lemma gives

det(Id+ΣS+κj​hj​hj⊤)=det(Id+ΣS)​(1+κj​rj),\det(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S}+\kappa_{j}h_{j}h_{j}^{\top})=\det(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})\bigl(1+\kappa_{j}r_{j}\bigr), (18)

while Sherman–Morrison gives

(Id+ΣS+κj​hj​hj⊤)−1=ΩS−κj​ΩS​hj​hj⊤​ΩS1+κj​rj.(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S}+\kappa_{j}h_{j}h_{j}^{\top})^{-1}=\Omega_{S}-\frac{\kappa_{j}\Omega_{S}h_{j}h_{j}^{\top}\Omega_{S}}{1+\kappa_{j}r_{j}}. (19)

Substituting Eq. 18 and Eq. 19 into Eq. 11, and using bS∪{j}=bS+λj​hjb_{S\cup\{j\}}=b_{S}+\lambda_{j}h_{j}, the corresponding change in the unhalved quadratic form is

2​λj​uj+λj2​rj−κj​(uj+λj​rj)21+κj​rj=2​λj​uj+λj2​rj−κj​uj21+κj​rj.2\lambda_{j}u_{j}+\lambda_{j}^{2}r_{j}-\frac{\kappa_{j}(u_{j}+\lambda_{j}r_{j})^{2}}{1+\kappa_{j}r_{j}}=\frac{2\lambda_{j}u_{j}+\lambda_{j}^{2}r_{j}-\kappa_{j}u_{j}^{2}}{1+\kappa_{j}r_{j}}. (20)

Half of this, together with the change −12​log⁡(1+κj​rj)-\tfrac{1}{2}\log(1+\kappa_{j}r_{j}) in the determinant term and the new quality term log⁡Φ⁡(−qj)\log\Phi(-q_{j}), yields

Δj​(S)=log⁡L~​(S∪{j})−log⁡L~​(S)=log⁡Φ⁡(−qj)−12​log⁡(1+κj​rj)+2​λj​uj+λj2​rj−κj​uj22​(1+κj​rj).\Delta_{j}(S)=\log\widetilde{L}(S\cup\{j\})-\log\widetilde{L}(S)=\log\Phi(-q_{j})-\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\kappa_{j}r_{j})+\frac{2\lambda_{j}u_{j}+\lambda_{j}^{2}r_{j}-\kappa_{j}u_{j}^{2}}{2(1+\kappa_{j}r_{j})}. (21)

The greedy step adds the candidate with the smallest Δj​(S)\Delta_{j}(S). After selecting jj, the maintained state updates are

ΩS∪{j}=ΩS−κj​ΩS​hj​hj⊤​ΩS1+κj​rj,bS∪{j}=bS+λj​hj.\displaystyle\Omega_{S\cup\{j\}}=\Omega_{S}-\frac{\kappa_{j}\Omega_{S}h_{j}h_{j}^{\top}\Omega_{S}}{1+\kappa_{j}r_{j}},\qquad b_{S\cup\{j\}}=b_{S}+\lambda_{j}h_{j}. (22)

The remaining scalars rℓr_{\ell} and uℓu_{\ell} can be updated recursively as well. If gℓ=hℓ⊤​ΩS​hjg_{\ell}=h_{\ell}^{\top}\Omega_{S}h_{j}, then

rℓ←rℓ−κj​gℓ21+κj​rj,uℓ←uℓ+λj−κj​uj1+κj​rj​gℓ.\displaystyle r_{\ell}\leftarrow r_{\ell}-\frac{\kappa_{j}g_{\ell}^{2}}{1+\kappa_{j}r_{j}},\qquad u_{\ell}\leftarrow u_{\ell}+\frac{\lambda_{j}-\kappa_{j}u_{j}}{1+\kappa_{j}r_{j}}\,g_{\ell}. (23)

With all hih_{i} retained in memory, each greedy step costs O⁡(N​d+d2)O(Nd+d^{2}), so one forward pass costs O⁡(k⁡(N​d+d2))O\bigl(k(Nd+d^{2})\bigr) time and O⁡(N​d+d2)O(Nd+d^{2}) storage. A naive implementation that instead rebuilds and factorizes Id+ΣS+κj​hj​hj⊤I_{d}+\Sigma_{S}+\kappa_{j}h_{j}h_{j}^{\top} for every candidate costs O⁡(d3)O(d^{3}) per candidate, hence O⁡(k​N​d3)O(kNd^{3}) time, with the same O⁡(N​d+d2)O(Nd+d^{2}) storage.

A.3 Greedy marginal in the equal-quality limit

Suppose that every quality score equals a common value qq, so that λi=λ\lambda_{i}=\lambda and κi=κ\kappa_{i}=\kappa for every ii, and that the penalty term is dropped. Then Eq. 11 reduces to

log⁡L~​(S)=|S|log⁡Φ⁡(−q)−12​log​det(Id+ΣS),ΣS=κ​∑i∈Shi​hi⊤.\log\widetilde{L}(S)=|S|\log\Phi(-q)-\frac{1}{2}\log\det(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S}),\qquad\Sigma_{S}=\kappa\sum_{i\in S}h_{i}h_{i}^{\top}. (24)

Adding a candidate j∉Sj\notin S changes ΣS\Sigma_{S} by the rank-one matrix κ​hj​hj⊤\kappa h_{j}h_{j}^{\top}. The matrix determinant lemma, det(A+u​v⊤)=det(A)​(1+v⊤​A−1​u)\det(A+uv^{\top})=\det(A)\bigl(1+v^{\top}A^{-1}u\bigr) for an invertible AA, applied with A=Id+ΣSA=I_{d}+\Sigma_{S} and u=v=κ​hju=v=\sqrt{\kappa}\,h_{j}, gives

det(Id+ΣS∪{j})=det(Id+ΣS)​(1+κ​hj⊤​(Id+ΣS)−1​hj).\det(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S\cup\{j\}})=\det(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})\bigl(1+\kappa\,h_{j}^{\top}(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})^{-1}h_{j}\bigr). (25)

Subtracting Eq. 24 at SS from Eq. 24 at S∪{j}S\cup\{j\} and using Eq. 25, the factor det(Id+ΣS)\det(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S}) cancels and

Δj​(S)\displaystyle\Delta_{j}(S) =logΦ(−q)−12(logdet(Id+ΣS∪{j})−logdet(Id+ΣS))\displaystyle=\log\Phi(-q)-\frac{1}{2}\Bigl(\log\det(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S\cup\{j\}})-\log\det(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})\Bigr) (26)
=log⁡Φ⁡(−q)−12​log⁡(1+κ​hj⊤​(Id+ΣS)−1​hj).\displaystyle=\log\Phi(-q)-\frac{1}{2}\log\bigl(1+\kappa\,h_{j}^{\top}(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})^{-1}h_{j}\bigr). (27)

The first term of Eq. 27 is the same for every candidate, and x↦log⁡(1+κ​x)x\mapsto\log(1+\kappa x) is increasing since κ>0\kappa>0, so the candidate with the smallest Δj​(S)\Delta_{j}(S) is the one with the largest hj⊤​(Id+ΣS)−1​hjh_{j}^{\top}(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})^{-1}h_{j}. Moreover, (Id+ΣS)−1=κ−1​(κ−1​Id+∑i∈Shi​hi⊤)−1(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})^{-1}=\kappa^{-1}\bigl(\kappa^{-1}I_{d}+\sum_{i\in S}h_{i}h_{i}^{\top}\bigr)^{-1}, so this ranking is the RepExp rule of Section 2 with regularizer τ=1/κ\tau=1/\kappa.

Φ⁡(u)=∫|u|∞ϕ⁡(t)​𝑑t<1|u|​∫|u|∞t​ϕ​(t)​𝑑t=ϕ⁡(u)|u|,\Phi(u)=\int_{|u|}^{\infty}\phi(t)\,dt<\frac{1}{|u|}\int_{|u|}^{\infty}t\phi(t)\,dt=\frac{\phi(u)}{|u|}, (29)

and hence λi>|u|=−ci​qi\lambda_{i}>|u|=-c_{i}q_{i}. Taylor expansion around x=0x=0 now gives

B.2 Proof of Theorem 2

The submodularity of the exact pass probability is a standard property of the probability of a union of events [46], and we prove it here for completeness. The new result is that the surrogate keeps this property.

Definition 1 (Submodular function).

A set function G:2[N]→ℝG:2^{[N]}\to\mathbb{R} is submodular if, for every A⊆B⊆[N]A\subseteq B\subseteq[N] and every j∉Bj\notin B,

G⁡(A∪{j})−G⁡(A)≥G⁡(B∪{j})−G⁡(B).G(A\cup\{j\})-G(A)\geq G(B\cup\{j\})-G(B). (36)
Definition 2 (Monotone function).

A set function G:2[N]→ℝG:2^{[N]}\to\mathbb{R} is monotone if G⁡(A)≤G⁡(B)G(A)\leq G(B) whenever A⊆B⊆[N]A\subseteq B\subseteq[N].

Definition 3 (Normalized function).

A set function G:2[N]→ℝG:2^{[N]}\to\mathbb{R} is normalized if G⁡(∅)=0G(\varnothing)=0.

B.2.1 Submodularity of Exact pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k Probability

First, we show that the exact pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k probability is already a normalized monotone submodular set function. To see this, let 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} denote the event that response ii is correct. The exact pass probability can be written as

P⁡(S):=Pr⁡(⋃i∈S𝒞i).P(S):=\Pr\left(\bigcup_{i\in S}\mathcal{C}_{i}\right). (37)

For any A⊆B⊆[N]A\subseteq B\subseteq[N] and j∉Bj\notin B, the marginal improvement from adding response jj is

P⁡(A∪{j})−P⁡(A)\displaystyle P(A\cup\{j\})-P(A) =Pr⁡(𝒞j∖⋃i∈A𝒞i),\displaystyle=\Pr\left(\mathcal{C}_{j}\setminus\bigcup_{i\in A}\mathcal{C}_{i}\right), (38)
P⁡(B∪{j})−P⁡(B)\displaystyle P(B\cup\{j\})-P(B) =Pr⁡(𝒞j∖⋃i∈B𝒞i).\displaystyle=\Pr\left(\mathcal{C}_{j}\setminus\bigcup_{i\in B}\mathcal{C}_{i}\right). (39)

Since A⊆BA\subseteq B,

(𝒞j∖⋃i∈B𝒞i)⊆(𝒞j∖⋃i∈A𝒞i).\Bigl(\mathcal{C}_{j}\setminus\bigcup_{i\in B}\mathcal{C}_{i}\Bigr)\subseteq\Bigl(\mathcal{C}_{j}\setminus\bigcup_{i\in A}\mathcal{C}_{i}\Bigr). (40)

Taking probabilities therefore gives

P⁡(A∪{j})−P⁡(A)≥P⁡(B∪{j})−P⁡(B),P(A\cup\{j\})-P(A)\geq P(B\cup\{j\})-P(B), (41)

which is precisely the submodular function property. Moreover, P⁡(∅)=0P(\varnothing)=0, and P⁡(A)≤P⁡(B)P(A)\leq P(B) whenever A⊆BA\subseteq B. Hence the exact pass probability is normalized, monotone, and submodular. This conclusion holds for an arbitrary joint distribution of the correctness events and does not require any latent-variable model or conditional independence.

B.2.2 Submodularity of the Approximate Pass Probability

Now, we show that the approximation under the Gaussian latent model itself is a monotone submodular function. Note that, every approximation of a submodular function may not necessarily be submodular. Before, we proceed, let’s try to get an intuition on the fact that L~​(S)\widetilde{L}(S) indeed represents some notion of a probability. Conditional on 𝐟\mathbf{f}, each term of the product in L~​(S)\widetilde{L}(S) can be written as

gi​(𝐟):=Φ⁡(−qi)​exp⁡(−λi​hi⊤​𝐟−κi2​(hi⊤​𝐟)2).\displaystyle g_{i}(\mathbf{f}):=\Phi(-q_{i})\exp\left(-\lambda_{i}h_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{f}-\frac{\kappa_{i}}{2}(h_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{f})^{2}\right). (42)

Consequently,

L~​(S)=𝔼𝐟∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)​∏i∈Sgi​(𝐟).\displaystyle\widetilde{L}(S)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{f}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})}\prod_{i\in S}g_{i}(\mathbf{f}). (43)

Hence, for L~​(S)\widetilde{L}(S) to be a definition of some kind of failure probability of selection of correct elements conditioned on 𝐟\mathbf{f}, it would suffice to prove that gi​(𝐟)<1g_{i}(\mathbf{f})<1. Towards this, for a scalar qq, write

λ⁡(q):=ϕ⁡(q)Φ⁡(−q),κ⁡(q):=λ⁡(q)​(λ⁡(q)−q),\lambda(q):=\frac{\phi(q)}{\Phi(-q)},\qquad\kappa(q):=\lambda(q)(\lambda(q)-q), (44)

and define

β⁡(q):=Φ⁡(−q)​exp⁡(λ​(q)22​κ​(q))=Φ⁡(−q)​exp⁡(λ⁡(q)2​(λ​(q)−q)).\beta(q):=\Phi(-q)\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda(q)^{2}}{2\kappa(q)}\right)=\Phi(-q)\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda(q)}{2(\lambda(q)-q)}\right). (45)
Lemma 1.

For every finite q∈ℝq\in\mathbb{R}, one has 0<β⁡(q)<10<\beta(q)<1. Moreover, β⁡(q)\beta(q) is strictly decreasing in qq.

Proof.

Let Φ¯​(q):=Φ⁡(−q)=1−Φ⁡(q)\overline{\Phi}(q):=\Phi(-q)=1-\Phi(q) and put

v⁡(q):=λ⁡(q)−q>0,r⁡(q):=log⁡β⁡(q)=log⁡Φ¯​(q)+λ⁡(q)2​v​(q).v(q):=\lambda(q)-q>0,\qquad r(q):=\log\beta(q)=\log\overline{\Phi}(q)+\frac{\lambda(q)}{2v(q)}. (46)

Since Φ¯′​(q)=−ϕ⁡(q)\overline{\Phi}^{\prime}(q)=-\phi(q), we have

dd​q​log⁡Φ¯​(q)=−λ⁡(q).\frac{d}{dq}\log\overline{\Phi}(q)=-\lambda(q). (47)

Also, direct differentiation gives

λ′​(q)=λ⁡(q)​(λ⁡(q)−q)=λ⁡(q)​v​(q),v′​(q)=λ⁡(q)​v​(q)−1.\lambda^{\prime}(q)=\lambda(q)(\lambda(q)-q)=\lambda(q)v(q),\qquad v^{\prime}(q)=\lambda(q)v(q)-1. (48)

Consequently,

r′​(q)\displaystyle r^{\prime}(q) =−λ⁡(q)+λ′​(q)​v​(q)−λ⁡(q)​v′​(q)2​v​(q)2=λ⁡(q)2​v​(q)2​(1−q​v​(q)−2​v​(q)2).\displaystyle=-\lambda(q)+\frac{\lambda^{\prime}(q)v(q)-\lambda(q)v^{\prime}(q)}{2v(q)^{2}}=\frac{\lambda(q)}{2v(q)^{2}}\left(1-qv(q)-2v(q)^{2}\right). (49)

It remains to show that the expression in parentheses is negative. For this, let X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1). Using the fact that, 𝔼⁡[X∣X>q]=λ⁡(q)\mathbb{E}[X\mid X>q]=\lambda(q), and 𝔼⁡[X2∣X>q]=1+q​λ​(q)\mathbb{E}[X^{2}\mid X>q]=1+q\lambda(q), we get

𝔼⁡[X−q|X>q]=v⁡(q),𝔼⁡[(X−q)2|X>q]=1−q​v​(q).\mathbb{E}\left[X-q\ \big|\ X>q\right]=v(q),\qquad\mathbb{E}\left[(X-q)^{2}\ \big|\ X>q\right]=1-qv(q). (50)

Hence, it would suffice to prove that

12​𝔼​[(X−q)2|X>q]≤(𝔼⁡[X−q|X>q])2.\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[(X-q)^{2}\ \big|\ X>q\right]\leq\left(\mathbb{E}\left[X-q\ \big|\ X>q\right]\right)^{2}. (51)

To prove the above expression, consider

T⁡(x):=Pr⁡(X−q>x|X>q)=Φ¯​(q+x)Φ¯​(q),x≥0.T(x):=\Pr(X-q>x|X>q)=\frac{\overline{\Phi}(q+x)}{\overline{\Phi}(q)},\qquad x\geq 0. (52)

B.2.3 Greedy Guarantee

Since P~\widetilde{P} is normalized, monotone, and submodular (Section B.2.2), by Nemhauser et al. [32], the greedy solution satisfies the guarantee of Theorem 2. □\square

Appendix C Selection Behavior Across Budgets

Proposition 2 gives intuition for how PKTP moves from Linear Probe to RepExp as kk grows when the correlations are weak. This section makes the two ends of this behavior precise for a fixed correlation scale ρ\rho. PKTP starts from the empty set and repeatedly adds the candidate jj with the smallest log⁡L~​(S∪{j})−log⁡L~​(S)\log\widetilde{L}(S\cup\{j\})-\log\widetilde{L}(S), and we call this the surrogate greedy rule. At one end, the probe-style rule keeps the kk candidates with the largest qiq_{i}, as Linear Probe does. At the other end, RepExp is implicitly a greedy rule as well. After a random first pick, RepExp with regularizer τ\tau adds at each step the candidate that most increases logdet(Id+τ−1GS)\log\det(I_{d}+\tau^{-1}G_{S}), where GS:=∑i∈Shi​hi⊤G_{S}:=\sum_{i\in S}h_{i}h_{i}^{\top} is the Gram matrix of the kept representations (Section A.3).

We keep the notation of Corollary 1, with λ⁡(q):=ϕ⁡(q)/Φ⁡(−q)\lambda(q):=\phi(q)/\Phi(-q), κ⁡(q):=λ⁡(q)​(λ⁡(q)−q)\kappa(q):=\lambda(q)(\lambda(q)-q), λi=λ⁡(qi)\lambda_{i}=\lambda(q_{i}) and κi=κ⁡(qi)\kappa_{i}=\kappa(q_{i}). Then ΣS=∑i∈Sκi​hi​hi⊤\Sigma_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}\kappa_{i}h_{i}h_{i}^{\top}, bS=∑i∈Sλi​hib_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}h_{i}, and, as in Eq. 11,

log⁡L~​(S)=∑i∈Slog⁡Φ⁡(−qi)−12​log​det(Id+ΣS)+12​bS⊤​(Id+ΣS)−1​bS.\log\widetilde{L}(S)=\sum_{i\in S}\log\Phi(-q_{i})-\frac{1}{2}\log\det(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})+\frac{1}{2}b_{S}^{\top}(I_{d}+\Sigma_{S})^{-1}b_{S}. (78)

We now give an overview of the results of Appendix C and the assumptions they rely on.

C.1 Overview of Appendix C

Section C.2 states the three assumptions that the results rely on. The first is that most candidates, the bulk, have qualities drawn independently from a fixed bounded distribution, while a few candidates, the spikes, have fixed qualities above every bulk quality. In other words, the pool contains a few spikes whose quality is higher than that of any other candidate, while the bulk consists of lower-quality candidates drawn from a common distribution. The second is that the representations are hi=ρ​vih_{i}=\rho v_{i} with ‖vi‖2≤1\|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 for a fixed scale ρ\rho, and do not depend on the qualities. Thus ρ\rho caps how strongly two candidates can be correlated, since Cov⁡(𝐙i,𝐙j∣H)=hi⊤​hj≤ρ2\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf{Z}_{i},\mathbf{Z}_{j}\mid H)=h_{i}^{\top}h_{j}\leq\rho^{2}, as in Proposition 2, and the similarity between candidates carries no information about their qualities. The third is needed only for large budgets. There we minimize the objective over a family of size-kk sets, and we require these sets to be diverse, meaning that their representations point in all directions rather than being concentrated in a few.

Section C.3 shows that at small budgets the two rules agree when the gap between the kkth and (k+1)(k+1)th largest qualities, measured as log⁡Φ⁡(−q(k+1))−log⁡Φ⁡(−q(k))\log\Phi(-q_{(k+1)})-\log\Phi(-q_{(k)}), exceeds a constant multiple of k​ρ2k\rho^{2}, which bounds the correlation terms that kk picks can accumulate. The surrogate greedy rule then returns exactly the top-kk set of the probe-style rule, and if this condition holds at every budget up to kk, it also adds these candidates in the same order.

Section C.4 shows that at large budgets PKTP and RepExp optimize nearly the same objective. To see this, we average the objective of PKTP over the bulk qualities, for the diverse sets of the third assumption. Apart from a constant and an error that shrinks as kk grows, minimizing this average is the same as keeping the spikes and maximizing the RepExp objective. This is a statement about the objectives, and it does not mean that PKTP and RepExp pick the same set.

Section C.5 constructs an explicit model in which both results hold. It fixes one quality distribution and one correlation scale ρ\rho. In this model, the surrogate greedy rule follows the probe-style rule for every k≤3k\leq 3, while the large-budget result holds as kk grows.

C.2 Assumptions

We use kk for the selection budget, with 1≤k≤N1\leq k\leq N for a fixed candidate pool. The three assumptions below concern the quality scores and the representations of the candidates.

  1. (A1)

    Bulk and spikes. There is a fixed set O={o1,…,or}O=\{o_{1},\ldots,o_{r}\} of r≥1r\geq 1 candidates, the spikes. The qualities of all other candidates, the bulk, are drawn independently from a distribution 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} supported in a fixed interval [w0,w]⊆[−M,M][w_{0},w]\subseteq[-M,M] for a finite MM. The spike qualities are fixed, lie in [−M,M][-M,M], and satisfy

    qo1>qo2>⋯>qor>w,q_{o_{1}}>q_{o_{2}}>\cdots>q_{o_{r}}>w, (79)

    so every spike has a higher quality than every bulk candidate.

  2. (A2)

    Correlation scale. The representations are hi=ρ​vih_{i}=\rho v_{i} with ‖vi‖2≤1\|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 and a fixed 0<ρ≤10<\rho\leq 1. They are deterministic, so they do not depend on the bulk qualities. A small ρ\rho means weak correlations between candidates, as in Proposition 2. The small-budget result needs ρ\rho to be small compared to a quality gap, while the large-budget results allow any fixed ρ>0\rho>0.

  3. (A3)

    Diverse representations. For large budgets, we let k→∞k\to\infty along a sequence of candidate pools of sizes Nk≥kN_{k}\geq k, while the dimension dd, the spikes and their qualities, the scale ρ\rho, and the distribution 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} stay fixed. The large-budget results minimize the objective over a family 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} of size-kk subsets of [Nk][N_{k}] with the following properties. It is deterministic and chosen independently of the bulk qualities. It is nonempty for every sufficiently large kk, and every S∈𝒜kS\in\mathcal{A}_{k} satisfies

    c0​k​Id⪯∑i∈Svi​vi⊤⪯C0​k​Id,‖∑i∈S∖Ovi‖2≤B0,c_{0}kI_{d}\preceq\sum_{i\in S}v_{i}v_{i}^{\top}\preceq C_{0}kI_{d},\qquad\left\|\sum_{i\in S\setminus O}v_{i}\right\|_{2}\leq B_{0}, (80)

    where c0,C0,B0>0c_{0},C_{0},B_{0}>0 do not depend on kk or SS. The first condition says that the representations in SS cover every direction, with a total weight that grows linearly in kk, and the second says that the representations of the bulk candidates nearly cancel out. Different sets in 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} may contain different spikes.

C.3 Small budget kk: a quality gap yields the probe-style rule

This subsection shows that when the gap between the kkth and (k+1)(k+1)th largest qualities is large compared to k​ρ2k\rho^{2}, PKTP keeps exactly the top-kk candidates, as the probe-style rule does. We write

Λ:=maxq∈[−M,M]⁡λ⁡(q)<∞\Lambda:=\max_{q\in[-M,M]}\lambda(q)<\infty (81)

for the largest value of λ\lambda over the possible qualities, which bounds every λi\lambda_{i}. Order the realized qualities as q(1)≥⋯≥q(N)q_{(1)}\geq\cdots\geq q_{(N)}, and let SktopS_{k}^{\mathrm{top}} be the set of the kk candidates with the largest qualities. For 1≤k<N1\leq k<N, define

Γk:=log⁡Φ⁡(−q(k+1))−log⁡Φ⁡(−q(k)).\Gamma_{k}:=\log\Phi(-q_{(k+1)})-\log\Phi(-q_{(k)}). (82)

Since dd​q​log⁡Φ⁡(−q)=−λ⁡(q)<0\frac{d}{dq}\log\Phi(-q)=-\lambda(q)<0, we have Γk>0\Gamma_{k}>0 exactly when q(k)>q(k+1)q_{(k)}>q_{(k+1)}. This gap measures the quality loss from replacing the weakest member of SktopS_{k}^{\mathrm{top}} by the strongest candidate outside it. The next lemma says that adding a candidate jj to a set of tt candidates changes the objective by its own failure term log⁡Φ⁡(−qj)\log\Phi(-q_{j}), up to an error that grows with tt and vanishes as ρ→0\rho\to 0.

Theorem 3.

≤−Γk+(1+3​Λ2)​k​ρ2<0.\displaystyle\leq-\Gamma_{k}+(1+3\Lambda^{2})k\rho^{2}<0. (93)

By Eq. 93, every outside candidate is worse than an available inside candidate. Starting with the empty set and inducting therefore proves that the first kk selections form SktopS_{k}^{\mathrm{top}}.

For global optimality, take a size-kk set R≠SktopR\neq S_{k}^{\mathrm{top}}. There exist j∈R∖Sktopj\in R\setminus S_{k}^{\mathrm{top}} and i∈Sktop∖Ri\in S_{k}^{\mathrm{top}}\setminus R. This proves uniqueness of the optimizing set, even if some qualities within SktopS_{k}^{\mathrm{top}} are tied. ∎

Applying Theorem 3 at every budget up to kk shows that the surrogate greedy rule also adds these candidates in the probe-style order, as long as every gap up to position kk is large enough. The spikes give such gaps, which leads to the following corollary.

Corollary 2.

Under (A1) and (A2), suppose 1≤r<N1\leq r<N and define

Γ∗:=min⁡({log⁡Φ⁡(−qoj+1)−log⁡Φ⁡(−qoj):1≤j<r}∪{log⁡Φ⁡(−w)−log⁡Φ⁡(−qor)})>0.\Gamma_{*}:=\min\left(\{\log\Phi(-q_{o_{j+1}})-\log\Phi(-q_{o_{j}}):1\leq j<r\}\cup\{\log\Phi(-w)-\log\Phi(-q_{o_{r}})\}\right)>0. (94)

If r​ρ2≤1r\rho^{2}\leq 1 and (1+3​Λ2)​r​ρ2<Γ∗(1+3\Lambda^{2})r\rho^{2}<\Gamma_{*}, then, for every realization of the bulk qualities, the first rr selections of the surrogate greedy rule are o1,…,oro_{1},\ldots,o_{r} in the order selected by the probe-style rule.

Proof.

All bulk qualities are at most ww. Thus the top rr candidates are the ordered spikes, and each of the gaps Γ1,…,Γr\Gamma_{1},\ldots,\Gamma_{r} is at least Γ∗\Gamma_{*}. Apply Theorem 3 separately at each budget k≤rk\leq r. The nested top-kk sets identify the full greedy order. ∎

The spikes are what keep this result meaningful in large pools. With bulk qualities alone, the gap between the kkth and (k+1)(k+1)th largest qualities typically shrinks as the pool grows, so the condition of Theorem 3 eventually fails. The gaps around the spikes do not depend on the bulk, so Corollary 2 holds for every pool size, while the bulk qualities keep a fixed variance.

The penalty term does not vanish, but on average it contributes the same constant d​vλ/(2​κ¯)d\,v_{\lambda}/(2\overline{\kappa}) to every diverse set. The spike term in Eq. 96, in contrast, depends on which spikes SS keeps, so it cannot be dropped while keeping a spike is still a choice.

When the large-budget optimizer includes the spikes.

Theorem 4 holds whichever spikes a set contains. To show that the best sets keep all the spikes, we need one more condition on 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k}, namely that a missing spike can always be swapped in for a bulk candidate.

Definition 4 (Closure under insertion of a missing spike).

A family 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} of size-kk subsets has the required closure property if, whenever S∈𝒜kS\in\mathcal{A}_{k} and o∈O∖So\in O\setminus S, there is a bulk candidate i∈S∖Oi\in S\setminus O such that

S′=(S∖{i})∪{o}∈𝒜k.S^{\prime}=(S\setminus\{i\})\cup\{o\}\in\mathcal{A}_{k}. (109)

This condition only requires one permissible replacement for each missing spike. It is not automatic for a family defined only by the diversity conditions, and Section C.5 gives a concrete family for which it holds.

Lemma 3 (The averaged objective keeps the spikes).

Suppose r≥1r\geq 1, every spike has a fixed quality qo>wq_{o}>w, and 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k} satisfies Definition 4. Under the assumptions of Theorem 4, every minimizer of 𝔼​log⁡L~​(S)\mathbb{E}\log\widetilde{L}(S) over S∈𝒜kS\in\mathcal{A}_{k} contains all of OO for all sufficiently large kk.

Proof.

We first bound the effect of one replacement on a log determinant. Suppose S′=(S∖{i})∪{o}S^{\prime}=(S\setminus\{i\})\cup\{o\}, where ii is a bulk candidate, and both S,S′∈𝒜kS,S^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}_{k}. Fix ν>0\nu>0 and set

A⁡(t)=Id+ν⁡((1−t)​GS+t​GS′),0≤t≤1.A(t)=I_{d}+\nu\bigl((1-t)G_{S}+tG_{S^{\prime}}\bigr),\qquad 0\leq t\leq 1. (110)

The uniform covariance lower bound gives A⁡(t)⪰(1+ν​c​k)​IdA(t)\succeq(1+\nu ck)I_{d} for some fixed c>0c>0. Also GS′−GS=ho​ho⊤−hi​hi⊤G_{S^{\prime}}-G_{S}=h_{o}h_{o}^{\top}-h_{i}h_{i}^{\top}, so

|dd​t​log​detA⁡(t)|\displaystyle\left|\frac{d}{dt}\log\det A(t)\right| =ν​|ho⊤​A​(t)−1​ho−hi⊤​A​(t)−1​hi|≤ν⁡(‖ho‖22+‖hi‖22)1+ν​c​k≤2​ν​ρ21+ν​c​k.\displaystyle=\nu\left|h_{o}^{\top}A(t)^{-1}h_{o}-h_{i}^{\top}A(t)^{-1}h_{i}\right|\leq\frac{\nu(\|h_{o}\|_{2}^{2}+\|h_{i}\|_{2}^{2})}{1+\nu ck}\leq\frac{2\nu\rho^{2}}{1+\nu ck}. (111)

Integrating over t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] shows, uniformly in the permissible replacement,

|logdet(Id+νGS′)−logdet(Id+νGS)|=O(k−1).\left|\log\det(I_{d}+\nu G_{S^{\prime}})-\log\det(I_{d}+\nu G_{S})\right|=O(k^{-1}). (112)

Recall that c¯=𝔼q∼𝒟q​log⁡Φ⁡(−q)\overline{c}=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\log\Phi(-q). Since q≤w<qoq\leq w<q_{o} almost surely under q∼𝒟qq\sim\mathcal{D}_{q} and q↦log⁡Φ⁡(−q)q\mapsto\log\Phi(-q) is strictly decreasing,

η:=mino∈O⁡(c¯−log⁡Φ⁡(−qo))>0.\eta:=\min_{o\in O}\bigl(\overline{c}-\log\Phi(-q_{o})\bigr)>0. (113)

The set OO is finite, so this minimum is a fixed positive number. If SS misses spike oo, choose the replacement supplied by the closure condition. The expansion in Theorem 4 and Eq. 112, with ν=κ¯\nu=\overline{\kappa}, give

𝔼​log⁡L~​(S′)−𝔼​log⁡L~​(S)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\log\widetilde{L}(S^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}\log\widetilde{L}(S) =logΦ(−qo)−c¯−12[logdet(Id+κ¯GS′)−logdet(Id+κ¯GS)]+O(k−1/2)\displaystyle=\log\Phi(-q_{o})-\overline{c}-\frac{1}{2}\left[\log\det(I_{d}+\overline{\kappa}G_{S^{\prime}})-\log\det(I_{d}+\overline{\kappa}G_{S})\right]+O(k^{-1/2}) (114)
≤−η+O(k−1/2)<0\displaystyle\leq-\eta+O(k^{-1/2})<0 (115)

for all sufficiently large kk. The threshold is uniform over the family. Therefore no minimizer can omit a spike. ∎

Once all spikes are kept, the spike term is the same for every remaining set, so minimizing the average comes down to maximizing the log-determinant. The next corollary makes this precise.

Corollary 3.

Let 𝒜kO={S∈𝒜k:O⊆S}\mathcal{A}_{k}^{O}=\{S\in\mathcal{A}_{k}:O\subseteq S\}, and for ν>0\nu>0 let

Dν(S)=logdet(Id+νGS),Skdet(ν)∈arg​maxS∈𝒜kODν(S).D_{\nu}(S)=\log\det(I_{d}+\nu G_{S}),\qquad S_{k}^{\det}(\nu)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{S\in\mathcal{A}_{k}^{O}}D_{\nu}(S). (116)

Under the assumptions of Lemma 3, let S^klog\widehat{S}_{k}^{\log} minimize 𝔼​log⁡L~​(S)\mathbb{E}\log\widetilde{L}(S) over 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k}. Then, for all sufficiently large kk,

0≤Dκ¯(Skdet(κ¯))−Dκ¯(S^klog)=O(k−1/2).0\leq D_{\overline{\kappa}}(S_{k}^{\det}(\overline{\kappa}))-D_{\overline{\kappa}}(\widehat{S}_{k}^{\log})=O(k^{-1/2}). (117)

Lemma 3 places each optimizer in 𝒜kO\mathcal{A}_{k}^{O} for all sufficiently large kk. On this family, Theorem 4 has the form

𝔼logL~(S)=Ck−12Dκ¯(S)+ek(S),supS∈𝒜kO|ek(S)|≤Ck−1/2,\mathbb{E}\log\widetilde{L}(S)=C_{k}-\tfrac{1}{2}D_{\overline{\kappa}}(S)+e_{k}(S),\qquad\sup_{S\in\mathcal{A}_{k}^{O}}|e_{k}(S)|\leq Ck^{-1/2}, (118)

where CkC_{k} is independent of SS. Optimality of S^klog\widehat{S}_{k}^{\log}, compared with Skdet​(κ¯)S_{k}^{\det}(\overline{\kappa}), implies

12[Dκ¯(Skdet(κ¯))−Dκ¯(S^klog)]≤ek(Skdet(κ¯))−ek(S^klog)≤2Ck−1/2.\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[D_{\overline{\kappa}}(S_{k}^{\det}(\overline{\kappa}))-D_{\overline{\kappa}}(\widehat{S}_{k}^{\log})\bigr]\leq e_{k}(S_{k}^{\det}(\overline{\kappa}))-e_{k}(\widehat{S}_{k}^{\log})\leq 2Ck^{-1/2}. (119)

This proves Eq. 117. ∎

Since Dκ¯D_{\overline{\kappa}} is the RepExp objective with τ=1/κ¯\tau=1/\overline{\kappa} (Section A.3), the minimizer of the averaged objective nearly maximizes the RepExp objective among the diverse sets that keep all the spikes.

C.5 An explicit model with both regimes

This subsection constructs an explicit model in which the assumptions of Section C.3 and Section C.4 hold at the same time, for one fixed quality distribution and one fixed ρ\rho. Let NN denote the total candidate-pool size, and consider a nested sequence of pools as N→∞N\to\infty. Each pool contains the same three spikes O={o1,o2,o3}O=\{o_{1},o_{2},o_{3}\}, identified with the indices {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\}, and a bulk set ℬN=[N]∖O\mathcal{B}_{N}=[N]\setminus O of size N−3N-3. The pools may be coupled by taking one infinite sequence of bulk candidates and letting ℬN\mathcal{B}_{N} contain its first N−3N-3 members. Throughout the construction, the dimension dd is fixed. For the large-budget regime, fix any exponent α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and define the integer-valued budget schedule

k⁡(N):=⌊Nα⌋.k(N):=\left\lfloor N^{\alpha}\right\rfloor. (120)

In the small-budget part of this construction, k∈{1,2,3}k\in\{1,2,3\} denotes a fixed selection budget, whereas k⁡(N)k(N) is the budget used in the large-budget regime. We first choose the quality distribution, then fix the common scale ρ\rho, and finally construct the growing pools and their families 𝒜k\mathcal{A}_{k}.

For the quality model in (A1), draw the bulk qualities independently from 𝒟q=Unif⁡[−γ,γ]\mathcal{D}_{q}=\operatorname{Unif}[-\gamma,\gamma], once for the nested sequence of pools, and let the three spike qualities be

qo1=4​γ,qo2=3​γ,qo3=2​γ.q_{o_{1}}=4\gamma,\qquad q_{o_{2}}=3\gamma,\qquad q_{o_{3}}=2\gamma. (121)

Next, consider the small-budget quality gaps. Since q↦log⁡Φ⁡(−q)q\mapsto\log\Phi(-q) is strictly decreasing, the quantity

Appendix G Extended related work

Pruning rollouts at test time.

Test-time scaling generates many rollouts per problem and aggregates them [44, 3, 35, 48], and a growing line of work saves compute by stopping unpromising rollouts early. One family uses the model’s own confidence, such as token-level confidence or its self-estimate of success, to decide which rollouts to continue [30, 13]. Another scores partial rollouts with a reward model [36] or with a probe on the hidden states [54, 1, 25]. Yang et al. [51] concurrently use such a probe for a beam search over partial rollouts, pruning weak rollouts and branching new rollouts from the best prefixes. All of these score each rollout on its own and keep the highest-scoring ones, which is the pure exploitation extreme of Section 2. At the other extreme, RepExp [39] selects rollouts whose representations are least explained by those already chosen, without using their quality. PKTP sits between the two, since it models how the outcomes of the rollouts depend on each other and chooses the set with the highest predicted pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k.

Pass@kk as an objective.

Pass@kk is a standard evaluation metric for reasoning and code generation, and several works optimize it during training. Walder and Karkhanis [41] derive low-variance policy-gradient estimators for pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k, Chen et al. [8] use pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k as the reward to balance exploration and exploitation, and Chow et al. [10] fine-tune a model for best-of-NN inference. Chen et al. [7] reward a group of responses for both quality and diversity, measuring diversity by the determinant of their similarity matrix. These are post-training methods, while PKTP leaves the model unchanged and optimizes pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k at inference time by choosing which partial rollouts to continue. Concurrently, Wu et al. [47] also leave the reasoning model unchanged, but use pass​@​k\mathrm{pass}@k as the reward to train a planner that writes a different outline for each rollout before it is generated. They thus change how the rollouts are sampled, while PKTP takes NN independently sampled partial rollouts as given and chooses which kk of them to continue.

Related objectives: maximizing at least one success.

The same objective appears in information retrieval as the expected 1-call@kk, the probability that at least one of the top kk documents is relevant. Chen and Karger [6] optimize it greedily, and Sanner et al. [34] show that greedy optimization under a latent subtopic model of relevance leads to diverse rankings, in the same way that our latent factor leads to diverse kept sets. In Bayesian optimization, the batch probability of improvement is the probability that at least one point of a batch improves on the incumbent, and it is monotone and submodular, so it can be maximized greedily [46, 32]. Other methods balance quality and diversity with a hand-set trade-off, such as maximal marginal relevance [5] and determinantal point processes [22]. In contrast to these works, PKTP applies to partial reasoning rollouts, learns the joint distribution of their outcomes from their representations, and optimizes a closed-form surrogate that keeps the submodularity of the exact objective.
